concept.name: Capacity utilization
concept.definition: The percentage of an industry's productive capacity actually being used, published monthly by the Federal Reserve alongside industrial production for manufacturing, mining, and utilities. It is computed as actual output divided by an estimate of sustainable maximum capacity.
concept.intuition: It shows how much slack the industrial economy has: high utilization foreshadows bottlenecks and price pressure, while low utilization signals idle plants and weak investment.
concept.mechanics: The Fed divides the industrial-production index for each industry by a related capacity index built from survey and physical-capacity data, reporting the operating rate as a percentage and comparing it with long-run (1972-present) averages for total industry and each sector.
concept.formula: Capacity utilization = (Industrial production index / Capacity index) x 100.
concept.failure_modes: Capacity is unobservable and estimated, so utilization rates are revised materially; readings above the long-run average do not reliably trigger inflation when supply chains are global.
concept.misconceptions: 100% is not the practical ceiling in these data - 'capacity' is defined as a sustainable maximum level of output, so utilization reflects engineering and economic constraints rather than a literal physical wall.
concept.example: In February 2026 total-industry capacity utilization was 76.3%, about 3.1 percentage points below its 1972-2025 average of roughly 79.4%.

citations.source: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Industrial Production and Capacity Utilization (G.17)
